topics.title: Introduction and Key Definitions
explain: GST is an ad valorem tax, meaning it is calculated as a percentage of the value of supply.
Consideration covers payments in money or kind, but excludes subsidies given by Central or State Government.
Deposits count as consideration only when the supplier formally applies them toward the payment.
Money includes legal tender, cheques, and drafts, but excludes rare coins collected for numismatic value.
An agent acts on behalf of another person to carry on the business of supply or receipt of goods or services.
The recipient is the person liable to pay consideration, or the person who receives delivery when no consideration is paid.

flow.title: Identifying whether an inflow is consideration
steps: Payment received in money or kind
Check if it is a refundable deposit
If deposit, check if applied to supply
Check if subsidy is from Government
Exclude Government subsidies from consideration
Balance amount constitutes valid consideration

topics.example: A customer gives a 5,000 rupee security deposit for a broadband router; it is not consideration until adjusted against an unpaid monthly bill.
remember: Government subsidies are never part of consideration under section 2(31).
Coins held for their numismatic value do not qualify as money.
mistakes: Treating refundable security deposits as part of the supply value before they are adjusted.

quiz.q: Under section 2(31), which of the following is excluded from consideration?
o: Subsidy given by Central or State Government
Payment made by a third party
Monetary value of an act of forbearance
quiz.why: Section 2(31) explicitly excludes subsidies granted by Central or State Governments from consideration.

quiz.q: When does a customer's deposit become part of consideration for a supply?
o: At the time the deposit is received
When the supplier applies it as consideration
At the end of the financial year automatically
When the customer demands a tax invoice
quiz.why: A deposit is treated as payment only when the supplier applies it towards the supply.

topics.title: Related Persons under GST
explain: GST law defines specific relationships where parties are deemed to be related persons.
Officers, directors, or legally recognised partners in each other's businesses are treated as related.
Employer and employee are statutory related persons under the law.
Holding 25% or more voting stock or shares directly or indirectly makes entities related.
Direct or indirect control of one person over another, or joint control by/over a third person, creates a related party status.
Members of the same family, as well as sole agents or sole distributors, are deemed related persons.

flow.title: Testing for related person status
steps: Identify relationship between supplier and buyer
Check for employer-employee or partner status
Check voting shares ownership at 25% or more
Check for direct or indirect business control
Check if family members or sole distributor
If yes, value under special valuation rules

topics.example: A holding company owns 30% voting shares in both Company A and Company B, making Company A and Company B related persons under GST.
remember: The equity holding threshold to establish control is 25% or more of outstanding voting stock or shares.
mistakes: Assuming that a sole distributor is an independent unrelated party for valuation purposes.

quiz.q: What is the minimum shareholding threshold for a third person to make two entities related persons?
quiz.why: Holding or controlling 25% or more of voting shares makes both entities related under Explanation to Section 15.

quiz.q: Which of the following pairs is deemed to be related persons under Section 15?
o: Two companies sharing a non-executive independent director
quiz.why: Section 15 explanation explicitly specifies employer and employee as deemed related persons.

topics.title: Transaction Value as Value of Supply
explain: Section 15(1) states that the value of supply shall be the transaction value.
Transaction value is the price actually paid or payable for the supply of goods or services.
This valuation method applies only when the supplier and recipient are not related persons.
Additionally, price must be the sole consideration for the transaction.
Payable refers to the agreed amount that the buyer is obligated to pay in future.
Commercial wholesale rates or market prices are irrelevant if the actual transaction meets these criteria.

flow.title: Applying transaction value under Section 15(1)
steps: Verify supplier and recipient are not related
Confirm price is the sole consideration
Identify price actually paid or payable
Adopt this price as transaction value
Adjust for statutory inclusions and exclusions

topics.example: A cement manufacturer with a wholesale price of 7,000 rupees sells 1 MT to an unrelated buyer for 6,700 rupees; the value of supply is 6,700 rupees.
remember: Transaction value is accepted only if parties are unrelated AND price is the sole consideration.
mistakes: Using list price or market value when the actual agreed sale price between unrelated parties is lower.

quiz.q: Transaction value under Section 15(1) is acceptable only when:
o: Supplier and recipient are unrelated and price is sole consideration
Market value is identical to the invoice price
Goods are supplied on an ex-factory basis only
Payment is made entirely in advance in cash
quiz.why: Section 15(1) requires two conditions: parties must not be related and price must be the sole consideration.

quiz.q: A Ltd. sells goods worth market value 10,000 rupees to an unrelated buyer B for 8,500 rupees. Sole consideration is price. The value of supply is:
quiz.why: Under section 15(1), the price actually paid or payable (8,500 rupees) is the transaction value.

topics.title: Mandatory Inclusions in Value of Supply
explain: Taxes, duties, and charges levied under other laws (like municipal taxes) are added if billed separately, but GST and Compensation Cess are not.
TCS collected under the Income-tax Act is not includible because it is an interim levy.
Supplier's contractual liabilities paid directly by the recipient to third parties must be added to value.
Incidental expenses like commission, packing, inspection, and handling charged by the supplier are included.
Anything done by the supplier before or at delivery forms part of the taxable value.
Interest, late fees, or penalties for delayed payment received by the supplier must be added, treating them as GST-inclusive.

flow.title: Determining additions to base price
steps: Start with agreed contract base price
Add non-GST taxes, duties, and cesses
Add supplier expenses paid by recipient
Add incidental costs like packing and inspection
Add received interest or delayed payment penalty
Result is total gross taxable value

topics.example: A supplier charges 1,00,000 rupees for machinery plus 15,000 rupees for pre-delivery inspection; both items are added together to make the value 1,15,000 rupees.
remember: TCS under Income-tax Act is never included in GST value.
Interest or penalty for delay is added only when received, and is computed on a cum-tax basis.
mistakes: Adding waived delayed payment interest; notional interest is never included if not actually received.
Adding GST or Compensation Cess into the taxable base under section 15(2)(a).

quiz.q: Which of the following items must be included in the value of supply under Section 15(2)?
o: Municipal taxes charged separately on the invoice
Interest waived by the supplier for late payment
quiz.why: Taxes levied under other laws like municipal tax are includible under Section 15(2)(a), while TCS and waived interest are not.

quiz.q: A customer pays 5,900 rupees as delayed payment fee (inclusive of 18% GST). What amount is added to the value of supply?
quiz.why: Delayed fees received are treated as inclusive of tax: 5,900 x 100 / 118 = 5,000 rupees.

topics.title: Treatment of Subsidies
explain: Subsidies directly linked to the price of a supply are included in the taxable value of the supplier.
Subsidies provided by Central Government or State Governments are specifically excluded from value.
Non-government subsidies (such as those from NGOs, trusts, or holding companies) directly linked to price are added.
Lump sum or blanket donations not linked to individual unit prices are not included in taxable value.
If a list price is already net of a non-government price-linked subsidy, that subsidy amount must be added back.

flow.title: Evaluating subsidy inclusion
steps: Identify if subsidy is received for supply
Check whether directly linked to price
If not linked to price, do not add
Check grantor: Government or Non-Government
If Government subsidy, exclude from value
If Non-Government price-linked, add to value

topics.example: A notebook retails at 50 rupees, but an NGO pays 30 rupees per notebook so students pay 20 rupees; the taxable value of supply is 50 rupees.
remember: Central and State Government subsidies are never added to the taxable value.
Lump-sum donations for general welfare are not directly linked to price and are excluded.
mistakes: Adding general NGO grants received as lump sums that do not reduce specific product unit prices.

quiz.q: A supplier sells goods for 200 rupees after deducting a 100 rupee per-unit subsidy from the Central Government. The value of supply is:
quiz.why: Subsidies provided by Central or State Governments are excluded from the value of supply under section 15(2)(e).

quiz.q: A trust gives a price-linked subsidy of 50 rupees per unit to a seller. The net invoice price charged to the buyer is 450 rupees. Taxable value is:
quiz.why: Non-government price-linked subsidies must be added back to the net price (450 + 50 = 500 rupees).

topics.title: Exclusion of Discounts from Value
explain: Discounts allowed before or at the time of supply and recorded in the tax invoice are directly deducted from value.
Post-supply discounts are deductible only if based on a pre-existing agreement linked to relevant invoices.
The recipient must reverse the input tax credit proportionate to the post-supply discount credit note.
Secondary discounts introduced after supply without a prior agreement cannot be deducted from GST value.
For secondary discounts, the supplier can only issue a financial or commercial credit note without adjusting GST.
No Claim Bonus (NCB) in insurance policies is an admissible pre-supply discount deducted from taxable premium.

flow.title: Testing discount deductibility
steps: Determine discount timing relative to supply
If before or at supply, record on invoice
If post-supply, check pre-existing agreement
Verify discount links to specific invoices
Ensure recipient reverses proportionate ITC
Deduct discount from taxable supply value

topics.example: A dealer earns a 5% volume discount agreed before sale upon reaching 1,000 units; when the supplier issues a tax credit note, the dealer reverses ITC and the supplier reduces output tax.
remember: Pre-supply discount must appear on the invoice to be deductible.
Post-supply discount requires both a prior agreement and proportionate ITC reversal by the recipient.
mistakes: Reducing taxable value for unscheduled year-end secondary discounts that were never agreed upon prior to supply.

quiz.q: Which condition is mandatory for claiming deduction of a post-supply discount under Section 15(3)(b)?
o: Discount must be in terms of an agreement existing at or before supply
Buyer must make payment in cash within 24 hours
Supplier must obtain prior permission from the GST Commissioner
Discount must exceed 10% of total invoice value
quiz.why: Section 15(3)(b) requires an agreement entered into at or before the time of supply specifically linked to invoices.

quiz.q: How is 'No Claim Bonus' (NCB) allowed by motor insurance companies treated under GST?
o: Treated as an illegal rebate and taxed
Deductible under Section 15(3)(a) as pre-disclosed discount
Added to premium as incidental income
Ignored and GST paid on gross premium
quiz.why: CBIC Circular clarifies NCB is disclosed beforehand in policy docs and invoice, hence deductible under section 15(3)(a).

topics.title: Supplies Where Section 15(1) Does Not Apply
explain: Section 15(1) fails when the supplier and recipient are related persons.
It also fails when price is not the sole consideration, such as in barter or exchange transactions.
In these cases, value is determined under Section 15(4) read with Chapter IV Valuation Rules of CGST Rules.
Section 15(5) empowers the Government to notify specific supplies whose value must follow prescribed rules regardless of price.
Detailed valuation rules (such as open market value or cost plus 10%) apply in these non-standard cases.

flow.title: Valuation route decision tree
steps: Check if parties are related
Check if price is the sole consideration
If unrelated and price sole, apply Section 15(1)
If related or non-monetary consideration present
Apply valuation rules under Section 15(4)
For notified supplies, apply Section 15(5)

topics.example: A company sells a laptop to its employee at a nominal price of 5,000 rupees; because they are related persons, value cannot be 5,000 rupees and must be determined via valuation rules.
remember: Whenever price is not the sole consideration, Section 15(1) cannot be used.
Notified supplies under Section 15(5) follow valuation rules even if transaction value exists.
mistakes: Attempting to value supplies between related persons using Section 15(1) transaction value.

quiz.q: When price is not the sole consideration for a supply, valuation is determined under:
o: Section 15(4) read with CGST Valuation Rules
quiz.why: Section 15(4) specifies that if value cannot be determined under Section 15(1), it must be determined under prescribed rules.

quiz.q: Which sub-section empowers the Government to notify specific supplies for determination of value through prescribed rules?
quiz.why: Section 15(5) allows notifying specific classes of supplies whose valuation is governed by prescribed rules.
